turn_text: Welcome back, everyone. We have Congressman Kat Kamik with us today. Thank you so much for being with us, Congresswoman.
Absolutely. Thank you so much for having me.

Well, tell us what it means to be the youngest Republican woman in Congress and tell us a little bit about how you got there from high school, college, working in politics and then running for office.

Well, it's an incredible honor to be the youngest Republican woman in Congress. It is such a humbling experience. And every time I walk through the halls of the Capitol, I get chills because you think of all of the greats that come before you and how you have a very, very big set of shoes to fill. And as you go to vote, sometimes you walk through Statuary Hall, and that's where John Quincy Adams had his desk at one point in time. And you think of the challenges that they faced in their day, and you look at what we're dealing with today. And it gives you the motivation that, hey, we've seen some tough times before, but we can definitely rise above. And I feel now more than ever that we need young people, we need millennials, we need Gen Zs at the table. When you look at the voting patterns, right, you have these, these blocks of folks millennials Gen Z's that when put together are the largest voting block in America, coming up. And so it's important that we have representation we have. a seat at the table, multiple seats at the table, but there needs to be a recognition of the fact that the policies that we're enacting today and the policies that have been for the last decade, two decades, they're not falling on the shoulders of baby boomers, they're falling on the shoulders of us. And so that's why it's important that we get involved now. And that relationship between our fellow Americans that are a little bit older than us is more important than ever, because it used to be, you know, they would make decisions. And it would take a long time for these things to enact. Well, things are moving so rapidly now that a $1.9 trillion stimulus package has immediate impacts for us here in America, and particularly young people as we're getting started, buying homes and starting families and going to grad school or starting out in the workforce, whatever it may be, that is something that is a direct, you know, all these decisions in Washington have direct impacts and it's decisions in Washington that actually led me to getting involved in the first place because I never had really politics as a goal in mind, you know, I grew up daughter of a single mom, you know, working class family and My goal ultimately, I mean, I had a big dream. I wanted to own the Minnesota Vikings. That was my big dream. But, you know, my realistic dream was to, you know, go to college. I'm the first in my family to go to college and then take over the family business, you know, get involved in the oil and gas industry. I'm originally from Denver. And that's a big industry in Colorado. So after college, I was thinking, yeah, that's going to be great. Well, I Didn't have that opportunity, let's say. You know, in college, I worked my entire way through. I was a bank teller for a while. I took a full load of classes. I was taking sometimes 16 credit hours. At one point, I did something ridiculous and I took 21 credit hours. I got a waiver and I was working a full time job. And I don't think that that was a very good idea. And I don't recommend that. So please don't do that. But working at the same time that you're going to school is such an important thing. And I did that through high school too. And so it gives you a bit of a work ethic. And it teaches you that you have to be responsible. And that's so important. But I get to the end of my college career. It's April. It's 2011. I'm getting ready to graduate. And my whole world falls apart. My mom got a phone call that we were losing our family's home, which was a small cattle ranch south of Denver. It was kind of like a bomb just went off in your little world, you know, everything around you still moving, but you know, your whole world has just, you know, been blown into pieces. Yeah. And so it was a pretty surreal experience of 23 days to evict. We have no money. I mean, I was paying for gas with like nickels and dimes and quarters. And I don't recommend that because at the time, gas station attendants, they hated that. They absolutely hated that. And so it was a challenging time for sure. We ended up moving into an extended stay motel and lived there for four and a half months. And it was a really challenging time. You're homeless. And the job market is crap. You're getting interviews, but you're not actually able to land a job because everything is a recession. And that's when I got a call from a family friend, and he said, my uncle's running for Congress in Florida. I think he'd be a good fit. And that's how I ended up in Florida. So, you know, unmarried and no kids, it was an opportunity of a lifetime to really pick up what I had and drive across the country and just take a chance on a guy who really had a passion to do something incredible for his country and I was so angry with big government because it was a big government program that ended up taking our ranch. It was a signature Obama housing initiative that was an 1800 page bill that no one had bothered to read and they ended up passing this legislation and what it did was incentivize big banks to push people out of their homes because it was a tax credit for every home that they couldn't save. You look at how government can impact people's lives so personally, it's not just, you know, taxes, it's not just regulations, it's people's livelihoods, it's the very homes that they live in and big government is dangerous and out of touch. And that's really what has inspired me into a life of service because I never want anyone else to feel that way. I never want anyone to experience a loss of everything that they have worked for their entire life. And so that's what has led me to today. And you talk about young people being involved. I think back to that election with Congressman Yoho and you know I was the only paid staffer and they really couldn't afford to pay me that much. And so let that be a lesson to you right there that you know you couldn't get offered a job and it may be like 500 bucks a month and in my case I think I made like 800 bucks a month or something and not really enough to live off of right so I was living in the guest house. If you are doing something that you're passionate about and you're motivated and it moves you to get up every morning and and it's driving you to to really do something incredible and meaningful. The money will come. Don't ever take on a job because you're like, oh, I'm going to make a ton of money, but I'm going to be miserable, right? That's something that I've seen a lot of really incredible people turn away from their passion of wanting to serve or do something because they're scared. that they're turning away money. And that's just, that's really sad. So, I've made a career now of being an advocate for people in my community. It's incredible to be the youngest Republican woman because I think that there's definitely a gap there. And I see a lot of young people in particular. We've been taught our whole life that you have to wait in line, you know, when we're kids and, you know, in kindergarten, what's the first thing your teacher tells you? Well, you know, we're going to line up and you're going to stand in a line and, you know, then you're going to go out to recess. So our whole lives were taught, were conditioned. stand in line, stand in line and wait your turn and I think now more than ever we need people who are willing to step out of line and say I feel very strongly about this and so I'm going to step out of line and take my shot and so that would be my number one piece of advice for for young people and I tell folks all the time that if come January 3rd of 2023 when I swear in as a sophomore in Congress. If I'm still the youngest Republican woman in Congress, then I have not done my job. I have failed my generation because I don't want that title for another two years. We need to have the next generation at the table. That's something that I'm adamantly focused on as part of my role in bringing the next generation of conservatives along with me for this ride.
